candidates.title: Track false-positive rate of self-generated tests before trusting a self-judged stopping rule
candidates.rule: Before relying on self-generated unit tests as the stop signal in an agentic coding loop, measure how often a solution passes all generated tests yet fails hidden tests; where that rate is high, the loop can end up below a single-shot baseline.
candidates.passage: the false positive test execution rate for MBPP Python is 16.3% while the rate for HumanEval Python is a mere 1.4%
candidates.finding: The paper links the loop's loss on MBPP Python (0.77 vs 0.80 baseline) to a much higher false-positive rate of self-generated tests than on HumanEval Python (0.91 vs 0.80), where the rate was low.
candidates.conditions: Up to 6 chain-of-thought-generated unit tests per problem, AST-filtered; pass@1 reporting without access to hidden tests
candidates.limitations: The causal link between false-positive rate and the MBPP regression is the authors' interpretation of one benchmark pair, not a controlled experiment; rates are model- and benchmark-specific and may differ for impure, non-deterministic, or API-calling functions as the authors note.
candidates.validation_test: On a target task distribution, generate test suites, then compute P(fails hidden tests | passes generated tests); compare loop accuracy to single-shot accuracy and check whether high false-positive subsets are where the loop loses.

reason: The paper reports ablations and null results that support narrowly scoped rules about retry loops: self-reflection plus self-generated tests, and settings where the loop does not help (WebShop, weak base model). Headline benchmark gains alone are not actionable, so proposals are restricted to the tested comparisons.
